prompt: Before r1 had any address, pc1's neighbour table held `10.20.10.1 dev eth0 INCOMPLETE`. What does that entry say?
hint: 10.20.10.1 is pc1's gateway.

choices.text: The gateway answered with an incomplete MAC address
choices.why: A MAC is all or nothing. INCOMPLETE means no answer came at all.

choices.text: Nobody answered pc1's ARP for its gateway
choices.why: Right. Nothing in VLAN 10 owned 10.20.10.1 yet.

choices.text: pc1 has no gateway configured
choices.why: It has one, 10.20.10.1, which is why it asked for that address.

choices.text: The switch blocked ARP between pc1 and pc2
choices.why: pc1 never asked for pc2's MAC. pc2 is in another subnet, so pc1 asked for its gateway's.

prompt: With no router yet, pc1 reached srv but not pc2. What made the difference?
hint: Compare their VLANs and their subnets.

choices.text: srv runs a web server and pc2 does not
choices.why: A ping does not care what services a machine runs.

choices.text: pc2 was not plugged in yet
choices.why: pc2 was plugged into p2 and answers as soon as a router exists.

choices.text: srv's port is a trunk
choices.why: srv's port, p3, is an access port in VLAN 10. The trunk is p8.

choices.text: srv is in pc1's VLAN; pc2 is not
choices.why: Right. Within a VLAN and its subnet the switch delivers; between VLANs a router has to.

prompt: Which of these route between two VLANs? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three were named in this lesson.

choices.text: A router with one port and one cable per VLAN
choices.why: It works, at the cost of a port per VLAN on each side.

choices.text: Adding both VLANs to every access port
choices.why: A port in two VLANs is not an access port, and the hosts would still send to a gateway nobody owns.

choices.text: A router on a stick, with one port on a trunk
choices.why: One address per VLAN on one physical port.

choices.text: Putting both VLANs' hosts in one subnet
choices.why: Then the hosts send ARP into a VLAN that does not hold the other half, and nothing is routed at all.

choices.text: A layer 3 switch with an interface in each VLAN
choices.why: The routing moves inside the switch.

prompt: 10.20.20.22 is outside pc1's own subnet, so pc1 hands the packet to its default ___.
hint: 10.20.10.1, for every machine in VLAN 10.

prompt: What does r1's `eth0.10` do?
hint: It is a VLAN interface on top of eth0.

choices.text: It is VLAN 10's interface: tags off coming in, on going out
choices.why: Right. Each VLAN gets an interface of its own on the one physical port.

choices.text: It is a second physical port, reserved for VLAN 10's traffic
choices.why: r1 has one port, eth0. The `@eth0` in the listing says what eth0.10 rides on.

choices.text: It copies every frame arriving on eth0 into VLAN 10
choices.why: Only frames tagged 10 reach it. Frames tagged 20 go to eth0.20.

choices.text: It filters VLAN 10's frames out of the trunk
choices.why: It filters nothing; it is where VLAN 10 meets the router.

prompt: r1's routing table holds two routes, and nobody typed either. Why was nothing more needed?
hint: Read `proto kernel scope link`.

choices.text: The switch sent r1 the list of its VLANs and subnets
choices.why: A switch tells a router nothing about routes; r1 learnt them from its own addresses.

choices.text: A default route already covers both subnets
choices.why: r1 has no default route. Both lines name one subnet each.

choices.text: r1 is directly connected to both subnets
choices.why: Right. An address with a mask brings its connected route with it.

choices.text: OSPF learnt them from sw1
choices.why: No routing protocol runs in this lab, and sw1 was not routing yet.

prompt: pc1 ran `traceroute -n 10.20.20.22` through r1. How many hops did it print?
hint: The router, then the destination.

prompt: A VLAN 30 with 10.20.30.0/24 is added to the switch, to an access port and to the trunk p8, and its hosts use 10.20.30.1 as their gateway. What has to be added on r1?
hint: One interface per VLAN, one address per interface.

choices.text: A second cable from r1 to the switch
choices.why: The trunk already carries VLAN 30. That is the point of the stick.
10.20.10.1 is r1 itself. The route appears on its own once r1 has an address in that subnet.

choices.text: An eth0.30 interface holding 10.20.30.1/24
choices.why: Right. VLAN 30's gateway, on the same port as the other two.

choices.text: Nothing: eth0 already sees VLAN 30
choices.why: It sees them tagged 30, and with no interface for VLAN 30 they have nowhere to go.

prompt: Match each piece of the router on a stick to its role.
hint: One cable, one port, two gateways.

pairs.right: r1's one physical port, on the trunk
the switch port carrying both VLANs tagged

prompt: How many ICMP frames did tcpdump capture on p8 for one ping from pc1 to pc2?
hint: Request and reply, each up and down.

prompt: pc1 sends 50 pings to pc2 through r1, and all 50 are answered. How many ICMP frames cross p8?
hint: Four per ping.

prompt: Compare the first frame on p8 with the second. What did r1 change?
hint: Read the MACs, the vlan field and the IP addresses.

choices.text: The destination IP address, to pc2's
choices.why: It was 10.20.20.22 in both frames: pc1 addressed pc2 from the start.

choices.text: The MAC addresses and the VLAN tag
choices.why: Right. A new frame for a new hop: from r1 to pc2, in VLAN 20. The IP addresses stayed.

choices.text: Only the VLAN tag, from 10 to 20
choices.why: The MACs changed too: the source became r1 and the destination pc2.

choices.text: Nothing, sw1 changed it
choices.why: sw1 forwards within a VLAN. The move from 10 to 20 is routing, and r1 did it.

prompt: The stick between sw1 and r1 is a 1 Gb/s full-duplex link. Which statement about the traffic between VLANs is right?
hint: Every routed packet goes up and comes down.

choices.text: Each VLAN gets its own 1 Gb/s on the stick
choices.why: The VLANs share one cable; a tag does not add capacity.

choices.text: Traffic between pc1 and srv also crosses the stick
choices.why: They are in the same VLAN, so sw1 delivers it without the router.

choices.text: Routed traffic shares 1 Gb/s each way
choices.why: Right. Every conversation between every pair of VLANs uses the same two directions of one cable.

choices.text: A fast switch raises the limit above 1 Gb/s
choices.why: The switch's speed inside does not change the cable to the router.

prompt: Put the four crossings of p8 for one ping from pc1 to pc2 in the order tcpdump saw them.
hint: The request finishes its trip before the reply starts.
items: Echo request, pc1 to r1, VLAN 10
Echo request, r1 to pc2, VLAN 20
Echo reply, pc2 to r1, VLAN 20
Echo reply, r1 to pc1, VLAN 10
trap: Each packet goes up in its sender's VLAN and comes down in its receiver's.

prompt: sw1 had vlan10 at 10.20.10.1 and forwarding on, and pc1's first ping to pc2 still failed. Why?
hint: Compare the MAC in pc1's table with vlan10's.

choices.text: The switch needed a reboot to start routing
choices.why: No reboot happened. A gratuitous ARP was enough.

choices.text: pc1's cache still held r1's MAC
choices.why: Right. Its table still held 02:1f:23:e7:e9:d5 for 10.20.10.1, and r1 was unplugged.

choices.text: Two machines held 10.20.10.1
choices.why: r1 had been unplugged before the switch took the address.

choices.text: pc2 had no route back to VLAN 10
choices.why: pc2's gateway is 10.20.20.1, which the switch now holds as well.

prompt: What is an SVI on a layer 3 switch?
hint: Cisco writes it `interface Vlan10`.

choices.text: A physical port set aside for the routed traffic
choices.why: It is virtual: no port and no cable.

choices.text: A trunk between the switch and an external router
choices.why: That is router on a stick. An SVI needs no trunk.

choices.text: A VLAN with no access ports in it
choices.why: That describes the lab's native VLAN 999, from lesson 19.

choices.text: The switch's own address in a VLAN
choices.why: Right. vlan10 and vlan20 in the lab are SVIs: an interface each, holding the gateway's address.

prompt: Why did sw1 need `bridge vlan add dev br0 vid 10 self` and the same for VLAN 20?
hint: Read br0's line in lesson 19's listings.

choices.text: So the switch's own interfaces hear them
choices.why: Right. br0 was only in VLAN 1, and vlan10 and vlan20 sit on top of br0.

choices.text: To turn p8 into a trunk for both VLANs
choices.why: p8 was already a trunk, and this command names br0, not p8.

choices.text: To switch on forwarding between the VLANs
choices.why: That is `sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1`.

choices.text: To give br0 the gateway address 10.20.10.1
choices.why: The address went on vlan10, in another command.

prompt: An ARP message a machine sends about its own address, unasked, so that every cache in the VLAN updates, is called a ___ ARP.
hint: `arping -U` sends one.

prompt: `arping -U -c 1 -I vlan10 10.20.10.1` printed `Received 0 response(s)`. What does that mean?
hint: Nobody was asked anything.

choices.text: The announcement was lost on the way
choices.why: pc1's table changed to the switch's MAC right after, so it arrived.

choices.text: pc1 refused the new MAC
choices.why: pc1 accepted it, and its table shows 02:6a:dc:93:3b:8a.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong
choices.why: Right. An announcement expects no reply; the count of responses is zero by design.

choices.text: Another machine already holds 10.20.10.1
choices.why: Then that machine would have answered, and the count would be one.

prompt: pc2's ping to pc1 was dropped, and pc1's ping to pc2 worked. Which rule let pc2's replies to pc1 through?
hint: The replies travel from vlan20 to vlan10, like the dropped ping.

choices.text: The chain's policy, accept
choices.why: The drop rule matches vlan20 to vlan10 before the policy is reached.

choices.text: The rule that allows tcp dport 80
choices.why: A ping reply is ICMP, not TCP.

choices.text: None: replies are never filtered
choices.why: They would be, by the third rule, if the first did not accept them.

choices.text: ct state established,related accept
choices.why: Right. The replies belong to a conversation pc1 started, and that rule comes first.

prompt: The drop rule's counter read `packets 2 bytes 168`. How many bytes long was each dropped packet?
hint: The same size every ping in these lessons announced.

prompt: If the first rule, `ct state established,related accept`, were deleted and the others kept, which of the three tests would change?
hint: Follow each test's replies through the remaining rules.

choices.text: pc1's ping to pc2 would start failing
choices.why: Right. pc2's replies go from vlan20 to vlan10 and would meet the drop rule.

choices.text: pc2's curl to srv would start failing
choices.why: The requests match the port 80 rule, and srv's replies go from vlan10 to vlan20, which no rule restricts.

choices.text: pc2's ping to pc1 would start working
choices.why: Its requests still meet the drop rule.

choices.text: None, since the chain's policy is accept
choices.why: The policy applies only to what no rule matched, and the drop rule matches pc2's replies.

prompt: The rules were attached to the `forward` hook. What does that hook see?
hint: Through the switch, or to it?

choices.text: Every frame switched within a VLAN
choices.why: Frames inside one VLAN are bridged, and the routed-packet hook never sees them.

choices.text: Packets addressed to the switch itself
choices.why: Those go to the `input` hook.

choices.text: Packets routed between its interfaces
choices.why: Right. Traffic from one VLAN to another, which is what the policy is about.

choices.text: Packets the switch sends on its own behalf
choices.why: Those go to the `output` hook.

prompt: With VLAN 20 removed from p8, pc2's pings to 10.20.20.1 all failed while `ip neigh` showed `10.20.20.1 … REACHABLE`. What does the REACHABLE entry prove?
hint: A cache records the past.

choices.text: That the gateway is answering ARP right now
choices.why: If it were, the pings would be answered too.

choices.text: An answer from before the fault
choices.why: Right. The table is history and the ping is the test.

choices.text: That the fault must be in pc2's firewall
choices.why: Nothing points at pc2. The trunk listing found the fault.

choices.text: That r1 has moved to another VLAN
choices.why: r1 did not move. The trunk stopped carrying VLAN 20.

prompt: Put the checks in the order the packet travels, from the host towards the far side.
hint: Start at the machine that complains.
items: The VLAN of the host's switch port
The VLAN on the trunk, at both ends
The router's interface in that VLAN
trap: Filters come last because a packet only meets them once it has been routed; checking them first skips everything that could stop it earlier.

prompt: Match each reading to the fault it points at.
hint: Each was seen in this lesson or in lesson 19.

pairs.left: A drop rule's counter rises with each attempt
The trunk port's listing has no line for VLAN 20
pairs.right: VLAN 20 is missing from the trunk

pairs.left: The gateway's entry still holds the old router's MAC
pairs.right: A stale cache after the gateway moved

pairs.left: ARP for the gateway stays INCOMPLETE on one PC alone
pairs.right: That PC's port is in the wrong VLAN

right_distractors: The 802.1Q tag is four bytes long

prompt: A campus has heavy traffic between its VLANs, much of it large file transfers. Which design suits it better, and why?
hint: Where does each design put the routed traffic?

choices.text: Router on a stick: one cable is simpler
choices.why: Simpler, and every routed packet would cross that one cable twice.

choices.text: A layer 3 switch, which routes inside itself
choices.why: Right. No trunk to a router, so no shared cable for every routed packet.

choices.text: Neither: put every department in one VLAN
choices.why: That undoes the reasons for the VLANs and makes one large broadcast domain.

choices.text: Router on a stick with VLAN 1 untagged
choices.why: The native VLAN changes nothing about capacity.

prompt: With r1 as a router on a stick, pc1 sends 10 pings to pc2 and 10 pings to srv, and every ping is answered. How many ICMP frames cross p8?
hint: srv is in pc1's VLAN.

prompt: Before and after the move from r1 to sw1, traceroute printed `10.20.10.1` as the first hop. Why did nothing on pc1 have to change?
hint: What did move?

choices.text: pc1 learnt the new router from a routing protocol
choices.why: pc1 runs no routing protocol. It has one gateway, typed once.

choices.text: The switch copied r1's MAC address
choices.why: It kept its own, 02:6a:dc:93:3b:8a, which is why pc1's cache went stale.

choices.text: Its gateway's address never moved
choices.why: Right. Only the MAC behind 10.20.10.1 moved, and a gratuitous ARP told pc1.

choices.text: pc1 was given a new gateway by DHCP
choices.why: pc1's gateway is static in this lab, and it is still 10.20.10.1.
